title: Post-Homeric emissary transfer to Persia and Greece
statement: According to the canon, the creators placed emissaries ('angels') among the Persians and the Greeks to accomplish technology transfer during the era of those powers' domination of Israel, as a punitive inversion of providence; this engagement falls in the sixth to fourth centuries BCE and therefore post-dates the crystallisation of the Homeric poems, so it explains no Homeric or Hesiodic content.

includes: The canonical report at TBWTT-3:213–215: emissaries placed among Persians and Greeks for technology transfer, punishing Israel's lack of faith, with Michael heading the Persian delegation (reading Daniel 10)

The chronological corollary: Persian and Greek domination of Judea runs from the sixth to the fourth century BCE, centuries after the eighth–seventh-century crystallisation of the Homeric and Hesiodic poems
The consequence for source discipline: the emissary episode is a late, discrete instance of engagement and cannot serve as the mechanism behind any archaic Greek text
excludes: Any use of this record to explain Homeric or Hesiodic content; the chronology forbids it
Identification of individual emissaries with named Greek or Persian historical figures
Any claim about the mechanism or content of the transfer beyond what the canon states
Mainstream historical endorsement; the record is canon-derived and labelled accordingly

source_references.locator: TBWTT-3:213 (domination by Persians and Greeks as punishment; 'angels' placed to accomplish technology transfer); TBWTT-3:214–215 (Michael heading the delegation to Persia, quoting Daniel)
Daniel 10:13, 10:20 (Michael and the 'princes' of Persia and Greece — the passage the canon reads)

alternatives.statement: Daniel's princes of Persia and Greece are celestial patron-angels within Second Temple angelology, a theological development with no technology-transfer content.
The Daniel passage encodes the theological problem of foreign domination, not any historical intervention among Persians or Greeks.
The canon retrofits a modern technology-transfer frame onto a text whose composition context (second century BCE) it does not address.

revision_triggers: Inspection of the canon's fuller context materially changes the technology-transfer reading of TBWTT-3:213–215.
The chronological corollary is challenged: any argument dating the relevant domination era before the crystallisation of the Homeric poems.
Public prose derived from this record starts using the emissaries to explain archaic (pre-classical) Greek material, which this record excludes.
Claim woh-claim-0001 is revised or retired.
